title: Functions I
subtitle: First Recipes
martuIntro:
At the Institute we called these recipes. You write the steps once and give them a name. When you need them, you call the name.
Some recipes need ingredients. Some hand something back.
You have met recipes already: `def move_left():` at the cabin door, `perform_roll(die_size)` at the trap door. Recipes were the hardest wall in the campaign, for everyone. Today we take that wall apart, one stone at a time, yes?
goals: Tell `=` (a box) from `def` (a recipe), and know that making a recipe does not run it
Call a recipe with `()`, and replace `pass` with a real step, indented under the `def` line
Give a recipe ingredients (parameters), and use their names inside it so every call works
Hand a value back with `return`, catch it in a box, and know why a recipe with no `return` hands back `None`
Trace a call: what goes in, what each box holds, and what comes back
Store what one recipe hands back, then pass it on to another, like the dialogue prompt in Module 1
Hand back a comparison with `return roll >= needed`, and roll with `random.randint(1, die_size)`

items.title: Quick review: 2 questions, not scored
items.summary: Two questions from Units 1 and 2, before you start recipes. Nothing is scored.

questions.q: Which line asks a yes-or-no question: is `roll` the same as 20?

whyWrong.0: `roll = 20` puts 20 in the box `roll`. Read `=` as *gets*: roll gets 20. It asks nothing.

questions.explain: Read `==` as *is the same as*. `roll == 20` asks the question, and Python answers `True` or `False`. A single `=` puts a value in a box.

Python works out the right side first, with what's in the box now: 26 − 3 is 23. Then 23 goes back in the box. In math, x = x − 3 has no answer, but in Python `=` means *gets*: mana gets mana minus 3.

items.title: Recipes With Names
items.summary: Make recipes (functions) with `def`, call them, give them ingredients and hand answers back with `return`. Then rebuild the moving, dialogue and skill-check recipes you saw in the campaign.

exercises.title: A box or a recipe?
exercises.martu:
A [[recipe]] is a set of steps with a name. Python calls it a *function*. [[def]] makes one: `def say_steady():`, with its steps indented under it. Making a recipe runs nothing. In math, f(x) = 2x is a rule, but nothing is worked out until you write f(13).
To run the steps, you [[call]] the recipe: its name, then `()`, on a line of its own. `say_steady()` runs it once.
`=` makes a box (a [[variable]]) that holds one value. `def` makes a recipe that holds steps.
At the cabin door, `def move_left():` did nothing until the game called `move_left()`. Now you know why, yes?

anotherWay.label: Box and card side by side
anotherWay.text:
```text
box:    name = value
        holds one value

recipe: def name():
            step
        holds steps

call:   name()
        runs the steps
```

anotherWay.label: A jar and a recipe card
anotherWay.text: A jar holds one thing, like sugar. A recipe card holds steps: mix, stir, bake. Writing the card bakes nothing. You bake when you follow the card. Calling `say_steady()` is following the card.

anotherWay.label: What Python does
anotherWay.text:
1. `steadying_words = ...`: Python makes the box.
2. `def say_steady():`: Python reads the recipe and remembers it. It runs nothing.
3. The end of your code. Nothing called the recipe, so nothing shows in the Console.
4. Add `say_steady()`: now Python runs the recipe's step, and `Steady, now.` shows.

anotherWay.label: Not this
anotherWay.text: Not this: `def ("mana")`. `def` never makes a box. A box is `mana = 20`. A recipe is `def say_steady():` with its steps indented under it.

anotherWay.label: You've seen this
anotherWay.text: At the cabin door, `def move_left():` made a recipe. The game called `move_left()` when you pressed the left arrow. No arrow, no call, no step. Same here: no `say_steady()`, no words.
My recipes sit in a book on the mantle. They do nothing there. Only when someone reads one out loud does anything happen.

anotherWay.label: From math class
anotherWay.text: In math, f(x) = 2x is a rule. Writing the rule works nothing out. f(13) uses it, and you get 26. `def` writes the rule, and `say_steady()` uses it. One difference: a `def` line has no `=`, so `def double(n) = n * 2` is an error.

checkpoints.text: Add `say_steady()` on a new line at the bottom of your code, with no spaces in front. That line calls the recipe. You should see `Steady, now.` in the Console.
hints: Look at the bottom of your code, under `print("Steady, now.")`. Is there a line that calls `say_steady`?
A recipe's name with `()` after it calls the recipe, and Python runs its steps. In the Example, `def hum():` makes a recipe, and `hum()` on its own line runs it.
Write `say_steady()` on a new line at the bottom, with no spaces in front. To make a new line, click at the end of the last line and press Enter.

campaignLink.why: You saw this at the cabin door. Each `def` line made a recipe. The game called `move_left()` when you pressed the left arrow. Making the recipe never moved the party: only the call did.

exercises.takeaway: `=` makes a box. `def` makes a recipe. Making a recipe runs nothing: its name with `()` calls it.

predict.q: Before you press Run: what will this print?
predict.explain:
Only `Oogrish waits.` shows. The `def` lines make the recipe, and Python remembers it. The step inside doesn't run, because no line calls `say_steady()`.
If you press Run on your code now, it shows nothing at all, for the same reason.

exercises.title: Call it
exercises.martu:
The lines [[indent|indented]] under a `def` line are the recipe's steps. They belong to it, like the indented lines under an `if` in Unit 2, or the sub-points under a main point in an outline. One call runs all of them, top to bottom.
Give Gearshift's `barrier_report` a second step. Then call it.
A recipe needs at least one step. With no indented line under the `def` line, Python stops with an error.

anotherWay.label: The indent means: belongs to the recipe
anotherWay.text:
1. `def barrier_report():` starts the recipe.
2. Every line under it with four spaces in front is a step of that recipe.
3. The first line with no spaces in front ends the recipe.
4. `barrier_report()`, with no spaces in front, runs all the steps, top to bottom.

anotherWay.label: Inside and outside
anotherWay.text:
```text
def barrier_report():
    step 1   <- inside
    step 2   <- inside

barrier_report()  <- outside:
                     the call
```
Steps: indented under `def`. The call: no spaces in front, with `()`.

anotherWay.label: From English class
anotherWay.text:
An outline puts each sub-point under its main point, pushed in:
```text
I. Barrier report
   A. Barrier's holding.
   B. Visor dims.
```
A recipe works the same way. The `def` line is the main point, and the indented lines are its steps.

```python
def tidy():
```

exercises.title: Replace pass
exercises.martu:
[[pass]] means *do nothing*. It holds a spot, like a blank recipe card: the card has a name, `step_north`, but no steps yet. Python needs at least one line under a `def` line, so `pass` keeps the spot.
Replace each `pass` with the step its recipe's name asks for. The scout (the one who walks ahead of the party) moves with `scout.step("north")`. Keep the four spaces in front.
The last four lines of your code call your recipes, like the arrow keys did. Follow the numbered notes, one per step.

anotherWay.label: A map with four arrows
anotherWay.text:
```text
         north
           ^
 west  <  scout  >  east
           v
         south
```
Each recipe's name says which arrow. Its step moves the scout that way.

anotherWay.label: A blank card
anotherWay.text: `pass` is a blank recipe card. The card has a name, `step_north`, but no steps yet. Write the one step it needs.

2. Delete the word `pass`, and keep the four spaces.
3. Type `scout.step("north")` there.
4. Press Run. The last lines call the recipe, and the scout steps north. Then do the next one.

exercises.title: Ingredients
exercises.martu:
Some recipes need an ingredient: a named blank that each call fills in. It's like a sentence frame in English class: "____, get inside!" In `def warn(hero_name):`, the blank is named `hero_name`. Python calls it a [[parameter]].
When you call `warn("Lucky")`, you hand over `"Lucky"`. Python calls that an [[argument|argument (what you hand over)]]. For that call, `hero_name` holds Lucky.
Inside the recipe, use the name `hero_name`, never one hero. I test your recipe with heroes you never wrote, like `warn("Tester")`, so one line must work for every hero.

example.output:
Oogrish is ready.
Gearshift is ready.

anotherWay.label: The call table
anotherWay.text:
```text
call                hero_name
warn("Lucky")       "Lucky"
warn("Bomb Shell")  "Bomb Shell"
```
One recipe. Each call fills `hero_name` with a new value.

anotherWay.label: A fill-in card
anotherWay.text: A fill-in card says: "____, get inside!" Each time you read it out, you put a different name in the blank. `hero_name` is that blank, with a name of its own.

anotherWay.label: It is a box
anotherWay.text: `hero_name` is a box, like the boxes from Unit 1, and each call fills it. `warn("Lucky")` works like writing `hero_name = "Lucky"` right before the recipe's steps run.

1. `warn("Lucky")`: `hero_name` gets `"Lucky"`.
2. The step runs: `hero_name + ", get inside!"` is `Lucky, get inside!`
3. `warn("Bomb Shell")`: `hero_name` gets `"Bomb Shell"`, and the same step runs again.
When the clock nears the arc, I shout the same warning at each of you. Only the name changes. That is a recipe with one ingredient.

anotherWay.label: From math class
anotherWay.text: In math, f(x) = x + 3 has a blank named x. f(5) fills it with 5, and f(10) fills it with 10. `hero_name` is the x of `warn`: `warn("Lucky")` fills it with Lucky. The recipe's line uses the blank's name, never one call's value.

```text
def show_hit(base_damage, bonus):
```

exercises.martu:
Inside the recipe, use the ingredient names, never the numbers from one call. The numbers arrive only when the recipe is called. It's a formula, like area = length × width: the formula works for any rectangle, but the answer 12 works for only one.
In Unit 1 you showed your work with box names, not the answer. Same here: `base_damage + bonus` works for every call.
Two calls are written for you. One line inside the recipe must work for both, and for my test calls too.

anotherWay.label: The call table
anotherWay.text:
```text
call            base_damage bonus
show_hit(4, 3)  4           3
show_hit(8, 2)  8           2
```
`base_damage + bonus` is 7 in the first row and 10 in the second. `4 + 3` would be 7 in both.

anotherWay.label: Why does this work? The recipe can't know the numbers yet
anotherWay.text: When Python reads the `def` line, nobody has called the recipe yet, so there are no numbers. `show_hit(4, 3)` brings 4 and 3. `show_hit(8, 2)` brings 8 and 2. Type `4 + 3` inside, and the second call still shows 7.

anotherWay.label: A fill-in card
anotherWay.text: The card says: add ____ and ____. You fill in the blanks each time you read it. Write 4 and 3 on the card in pen, and every reading says 7.

anotherWay.label: Ingredients arrive at the call
anotherWay.text:
```text
show_hit(8, 2)
         |  |
         v  v
  base_damage=8
  bonus=2
  print(8 + 2) -> 10
```

exercises.title: Hand it back
exercises.martu:
[[return]] hands a value back to the line that called the recipe. Think of class: `print` is saying the answer out loud, and `return` is writing it on the answer sheet. `return total` hands back what's in `total`.
Lucky's affinity (how strong his magic is) is 13. Catch his max mana in a box: `lucky_max = max_mana_for(13)`. The call is replaced by what comes back, the way f(13) is replaced by 26 in math. If nothing catches it, it's gone.
A recipe with no `return` hands back [[None]], Python's word for nothing. It is not 0.
Try it if you like, after Step 2 (it's not a step): delete `return total`, press Run, and see what `lucky_max` holds. Then put it back.

anotherWay.label: The return arrow
anotherWay.text:
```text
lucky_max = max_mana_for(13)
    ^             |
    |    affinity = 13
    |    total = 26
    +--- return total
```
The answer comes back to the call, and the box on the left catches it.

anotherWay.label: Written down and handed back
anotherWay.text: You ask a friend to add up the bill. `print` is them shouting the total across the room. `return` is them writing it down and handing you the paper. You can keep the paper.

anotherWay.label: Step table
anotherWay.text:
1. `max_mana_for(13)`: `affinity` gets 13.
2. `total = affinity * 2`: `total` gets 26.
3. `return total`: the recipe hands back 26 and ends.
4. `lucky_max = ...`: the box catches 26.
5. `print(lucky_max)` shows 26.

anotherWay.label: Why does this work? `return` ends the recipe
anotherWay.text:
`return` hands the answer back, and the recipe stops there. A line under it, inside the recipe, never runs:
```python
def double(n):
    return n * 2
    print("Never shown.")
```
`double(4)` hands back 8 and prints nothing.

anotherWay.label: You've seen this
anotherWay.text: At the trap door, `perform_roll(die_size)` handed back a roll with `return`. The skill check caught it and compared it. A recipe that hands back is a recipe you can use again.
At the Institute, apprentices wrote their answers down and passed the paper up. A shouted answer helped nobody at the back. A written answer could be kept.

anotherWay.label: From math class
anotherWay.text: Think of a function machine. 13 goes in, the rule doubles it, and 26 comes out. `return` is the side where the answer comes out. In `lucky_max = max_mana_for(13)`, the call is replaced by 26, the way f(13) is replaced by 26.

exercises.title: Be the ledger
exercises.martu:
To *trace* a program, you run it in your head, one line at a time, like showing your work in math. A *ledger* is a notebook where you write down numbers. Trace this program, and write down what each box holds:
```python
def ward_strength(lanterns, runes):
    light = lanterns * 10
    glow = runes * 5
    return light + glow

barrier = ward_strength(3, 4) + 10
print(barrier)
```
Your code is the ledger: each row is one box. Change each 0 to what that box holds. Use what is IN the boxes at that moment, not the numbers written in the recipe.
Fill every row first. Then press Run to check your rows.

anotherWay.label: The return arrow, with another call
anotherWay.text:
Here is the same recipe with another call. Do yours the same way.
```text
ward_strength(4, 3) + 10
  lanterns = 4
  runes = 3
  light = 40
  glow = 15
  return 55 ----+
                |
barrier = 55 + 10
        = 65
```

anotherWay.label: Step by step, with another call
anotherWay.text:
Here is the same recipe with another call. Do yours the same way.
1. `ward_strength(4, 3)` hands over 4 and 3: `lanterns` is 4, `runes` is 3.
2. `light` is 4 times 10: 40.
3. `glow` is 3 times 5: 15.
4. The recipe hands back 40 + 15: 55.
5. `barrier` is 55 + 10: 65.
6. `print(barrier)` shows 65, and only 65.

solution: # The ledger: what each box holds
exercises.takeaway: Trace a call with what is IN the boxes. What the recipe hands back takes the place of the call.
exercises.pairTalk: Pair talk: fill your ledger on your own first. Then compare rows with your partner. Where do you differ? Find the line in the program that settles it.

exercises.title: Return the right box
exercises.martu:
A recipe can't hand back a box made somewhere else. `armor_total` makes `total`, so it hands back `total` with `return total`. A box made inside one recipe stays there, like a bowl that belongs to one kitchen.
This code has two [[bug|bugs]]. A loud one makes Python stop with an error. A quiet one runs, but `Shield:` shows `None`. Fix them one at a time.
When Python stops, read the error box in the Console: its title says what went wrong. Then read *Python's last line*, and go to the line number it gives.

anotherWay.label: Why does this work? Whose kitchen is `result` in?
anotherWay.text: `result` was made inside `triple`, in my Example. A box made inside a recipe lives in that recipe's kitchen only. `armor_total` has its own kitchen, and its box is `total`.

anotherWay.label: Two kitchens
anotherWay.text:
```text
triple's kitchen:
  result

armor_total's kitchen:
  total   <- hand this back
```

anotherWay.label: The wrong bowl
anotherWay.text: You cook soup in the blue bowl, then hand over the red bowl from yesterday's kitchen. It isn't here. Hand over the bowl you filled.

4. Press Run. `Shield: None` means the second recipe has no `return`. Add one.

exercises.title: Store, then pass it on
exercises.martu:
You can store what one recipe hands back in a box (a variable), then hand that box to another recipe. It's like basketball: you catch the ball, then pass it on. `greeting = get_greeting()` catches the line, and `show_on_ley_board(greeting)` passes it to the Ley board, a message board that shows it in the Console.
`get_greeting()` also tidies its line. `.lower()` makes every letter small, then [[.capitalize()]] makes only the first letter big, like Format, then Capitalization, then Sentence case in Google Docs.
You did these three moves in Module 1, yes? Call the helper (the recipe that hands back the line), store what it hands back, pass it on. Now you'll see why they work.

anotherWay.label: You've seen this
anotherWay.text: Module 1: `get_dialogue_prompt_string()` handed back Mar'tu's line. `present_dialogue_option()` stored it in a variable, then passed that variable to `print_prompt()`. Same three moves.

anotherWay.label: Three moves
anotherWay.text:
1. Call the helper: `get_greeting()`.
2. Store what it hands back: `greeting = get_greeting()`.
3. Pass it on: `show_on_ley_board(greeting)`.

anotherWay.label: Caught, then passed on
anotherWay.text:
```text
get_greeting()
   | hands back the line
   v
greeting  (stored)
   |
   v
show_on_ley_board(greeting)
```

exercises.title: Return a comparison
exercises.martu:
A comparison like `roll >= needed` (is the roll at least the number needed?) is a yes-or-no question, and Python answers it with `True` or `False`. So a recipe can hand back the answer itself: `return roll >= needed`. It's like checking an inequality in math: is 15 ≥ 12? True. `>=` means *at least*, like a filled dot on a number line.
The Example shows two ways to write a skill check: an `if` that hands back `True` or `False`, and one short line. They give the same answer.
Follow the numbered notes in your code, one per step.

anotherWay.label: You've seen this
anotherWay.text: At the trap door, each check set `required_roll`, then handed back `roll >= required_roll`. Same shape here, with `needed`.

anotherWay.label: The two forms are the same
anotherWay.text:
1. `roll >= needed` is a question. Python answers it: `True` or `False`.
2. The long form asks it in an `if`, then hands back `True` or `False` itself.
3. The short form hands back Python's answer straight away. Same result, one line.

anotherWay.label: A number line
anotherWay.text:
```text
1 ... needed-1 | needed ... 20
     False     |     True
```
`return roll >= needed`. Exactly enough passes.

anotherWay.label: From math class
anotherWay.text: In math, you check an inequality by putting in a number. Is 15 ≥ 12? True. Is 11 ≥ 12? False. `roll >= needed` is the same check, and `return` hands back Python's true-or-false answer.

exercises.title: A rolling recipe
exercises.martu:
Your recipe `roll_die` has one ingredient, `die_size`: how many faces the die has. 6 means a six-sided die (a d6), and 20 means a d20. In Unit 2, `random.randint(1, 6)` rolled a d6: any whole number from 1 to 6, both ends included. Put the ingredient where the 6 was, and one recipe rolls any die.
At the trap door, `perform_roll(die_size)` did this for every check. Now you write it yourself.

anotherWay.label: You've seen this
anotherWay.text: Module 2, the trap door: `perform_roll(die_size)` handed back `random.randint(1, die_size)`. Every check called it. One recipe, any die.

1. `roll_die(6)`: `die_size` gets 6.
2. `random.randint(1, die_size)` rolls from 1 to 6.
3. `return` hands that roll back to the line that called.

anotherWay.label: A die with die_size faces
anotherWay.text:
```text
roll_die(6)   ->  1 to 6
roll_die(20)  ->  1 to 20
die_size sets the top face.
```

anotherWay.label: From math class
anotherWay.text: In math, a fair die means every face has the same chance. `random.randint(1, 6)` picks one whole number from 1 to 6, and 1 and 6 can both come up. In everyday talk, *random* can mean weird. Here it means every number has the same chance.

This code has four [[bug|bugs]], and Python shows them one at a time. When it stops, read the error box in the Console: its title says what went wrong, *Python's last line* says it in Python's words, and the line number says where. Fix that line, then press Run again.
A new error after a fix is good news: Python got further. That's how everyone finds bugs, yes?

anotherWay.label: One mistake at a time
anotherWay.text:
1. Press Run. Read the error box in the Console: its title, then Python's last line.
2. Go to the line number it gives. Fix that line.
3. Press Run again. A new error? Good: Python got further, and that is the next mistake.
4. No error? Then Your steps tell you what is left.

```text
line 1  def steady_word()

line 4  def hours_left = 37

line 6  the call

line 10 return result

```

items.title: Recipe Quiz
items.summary: Recipe quiz: 8 questions on making, calling and tracing recipes. Retake it as often as you like.

questions.explain: `4 * 5` is typed into the recipe, so every call shows 20, whatever it hands over. `cells * 5` would show 35 for this call.
The call prints 26 while it runs. But the recipe has no `return`, so it hands back `None`, and `lucky_max` holds `None`. `print` shows a value on the screen. `return` hands it back.

questions.q: Trace it like the ledger in Be the ledger. What will this print?
questions.explain:
`lanterns` holds 2 and `runes` holds 8. `light` is 20, `glow` is 40, so the recipe hands back 60. Then 60 + 10 is 70.
60 forgets the `+ 10` on the `barrier` line. 50 starts from `glow` (40 + 10), not from what the recipe hands back. 25 adds the numbers written in the recipe (10 + 5 + 10). 20 adds the numbers handed over (2 + 8 + 10).
`>=` means at least. 10 is one short: `False`. 11 is exactly enough: `True`. 12 is more: `True`. The recipe hands back the answer, not the roll.

questions.q: In `warn("Lucky")`, which part is the argument (what you hand over)?

whyWrong.0: `warn` is the recipe's name. It says which recipe to run.
whyWrong.2: `hero_name` is the ingredient (parameter): the blank's name on the `def` line. It holds what you hand over during the call.
whyWrong.3: The parentheses make the call happen. What goes inside them is the argument, what you hand over.

questions.explain: The argument (what you hand over) is `"Lucky"`. During the call, the ingredient `hero_name` holds it.

questions.q: Put the lines in order (with their indents) so the program shows Mar'tu's greeting. Store it in a variable first, then pass it on.
questions.explain: Call the helper, store what it hands back in `greeting`, then pass `greeting` on. With no `()`, `get_greeting` is the recipe itself, not its line.

whyWrong.1: The recipe works out 14 in `left`, but it hands back `result`, a box this recipe never made.
whyWrong.2: `None` comes from a recipe with no `return` line. This one has a `return`, and it names a box that doesn't exist, so Python stops.

questions.explain: The box that `mana_after` makes is `left`. `return result` makes Python stop with an error: name 'result' is not defined. The fix is `return left`.
`double(4)` hands back 8, and `y` catches it. Then `y + 1` is 9.

items.title: Extra practice: Recipe twins
items.summary: Three short recipes shaped like the ones in Recipes With Names: one shows a line, one hands back an answer, and one hands back an answer you catch in a box.

exercises.title: Twin: cheer them on
exercises.martu:
This recipe has two [[ingredients]], `hero_name` and `words`. They are named blanks, like the sentence frame in Ingredients: "____: ____". Each call fills both blanks, in order. In `cheer_on("Lucky", "Fine. I'm in.")`, the first value fills `hero_name` and the second fills `words`.
It's a twin of `warn` from Recipes With Names: the same shape, with new names. Finish the recipe so each call shows its own hero and words. Then add a call of your own.

anotherWay.label: Who fills what
anotherWay.text:
```text
call 1: hero_name = "Lucky"
        words = "Fine. I'm in."
call 2: hero_name = "Oogrish"
        words = "Steady, now."
```
Each call fills both ingredients again, with its own values. The `print` line reads them.

anotherWay.label: A fill-in card
anotherWay.text: The card says `___: ___`. The first blank is for the hero, and the second is for the words. Each call writes new words in the blanks, but the card stays the same.

1. Python reads the `def` line and remembers the recipe. Nothing runs yet.
2. The first call puts `"Lucky"` in `hero_name` and `"Fine. I'm in."` in `words`.
3. The `print` line glues them, with `": "` in between.
4. The next call fills both ingredients again, with its own values.

anotherWay.label: You've seen this
anotherWay.text: At the cabin door, `party.move("left")` handed one value, `"left"`, to a recipe the game wrote. Here you write the recipe yourself, and each call hands it two values.

starter: # print the hero, then ": ", then the words
# should show: Lucky: Fine. I'm in.

checkpoints.text: Replace `pass` with a `print` line that shows the hero, then `: `, then the words. Glue them with `+`, using `hero_name` and `words`. You should see `Lucky: Fine. I'm in.` in the Console.
hints: Look at line 1, the `def` line. Which two ingredient names does it give? The note on line 2 says what order to show them in.
Inside the recipe, each ingredient's name holds what the call handed over. The Example glues two ingredients with `+`, like a compound word: `print(owner + "'s " + item)`.
Use the ingredient names, not one call's words. `print("Lucky: Fine. I'm in.")` would show Lucky for every call, even Oogrish's.
Write `print(hero_name + ": " + words)` in place of `pass`, four spaces in.

exercises.title: Twin: double the cost
exercises.martu:
This recipe [[hands back]] its answer with `return`. As in Hand it back: `print` says the answer out loud, and `return` writes it on the answer sheet. The ingredient `price` is the price of one thing, and the recipe hands back twice that: `double_cost(4)` should hand back 8.
The calls are already at the bottom of your code. `print(double_cost(4))` shows what the call hands back. Right now it shows [[None]], Python's word for nothing, because the recipe holds only `pass`.

anotherWay.label: The return arrow
anotherWay.text:
```text
print(double_cost(4))
      price = 4
      4 * 2 = 8
      return 8 --+
                 |
print(   8   ) <-+
```
`print` says the answer out loud to the room. `return` writes it down and hands the paper to whoever called. Here the one who called is `print(...)`, which shows that answer in the Console.

1. `double_cost(4)` puts 4 in `price`.
2. `price * 2` is 8.
3. `return` hands 8 back to the call.
4. `print` shows 8. Then the next call puts 15 in `price`.
`return price * 2`. Never a number from one call.

anotherWay.label: From math class
anotherWay.text: In math, f(x) = 2x is a rule, and f(4) = 8 works it out. `double_cost` is the same kind of rule: `price` is the x, and `double_cost(4)` is replaced by 8, the way f(4) is replaced by 8. One difference: Python needs the times sign, so write `price * 2`, never `2price`.

exercises.title: Twin: glug left
exercises.martu:
When a recipe hands back an answer, catch it in a [[box]], so later lines can use it. The call is replaced by what it hands back, the way f(13) is replaced by 26 in math. In the Example, `tonight = ward_cost(3)` puts 12 in `tonight`.
`glug_left` takes two ingredients: the sips Lucky has now, and the sips he drinks. It hands back the sips left. Glug is Lucky's drink, and his canteen is his water bottle. It heals, and it smells terrible.

anotherWay.label: Where the answer lands
anotherWay.text:
```text
sips_left = glug_left(9, 4)
            sips_now = 9
            sips_drunk = 4
            return 5
     <-- 5 lands here
```

anotherWay.label: Catch the package
anotherWay.text: The recipe hands you a package. If you don't put it somewhere, it's gone. `sips_left = ...` puts it on a shelf with a name on it, so a later line can pick it up.

1. `glug_left(9, 4)` fills `sips_now` with 9 and `sips_drunk` with 4.
2. It hands back 5.
3. `sips_left` catches the 5.
4. `print(sips_left)` shows it in the Console.

items.title: Lucky's Supply Run
items.summary: Turn Lucky's costs, worked out by hand, into one recipe that every cost line calls.
items.martu:
A cost is how many things times the price of one, like unit price in math: 3 lanterns at 4 coins each cost 3 × 4 coins. Lucky worked out the costs for his supply run (a shopping trip for supplies) by hand, and typed the total. If one price changes, he has to fix the lines by hand. A recipe does the math once, for every line: `item_cost(10, 2)` would hand back 20.
Write `item_cost`, make each cost line call it, and make `total_cost` add the three boxes. I test your code with other numbers, so every cost line and the total must change to match.

anotherWay.label: An online cart
anotherWay.text: Math scribbled on a paper receipt is wrong once a price changes. An online cart works it out again: change a number, press Update, and every line and the total change to match. Your recipe works like the cart, and ▶ Run is your Update button.

1. Write `item_cost(count, price)` at the top. It hands back the count times the price.
2. Change each old cost line to a call with the same two numbers.
3. Make `total_cost` add the three cost boxes.
4. Keep the `print` line as it is.

anotherWay.label: You've seen this
anotherWay.text: `perform_roll(die_size)` did the rolling once, for every check that called it. `item_cost` does the multiplying once, for every cost line.

anotherWay.label: From math class
anotherWay.text: A ratio table for lanterns: 1 lantern costs 4 coins, 2 cost 8, 3 cost 12. The rule under the table is cost = count × unit price. `item_cost` is that rule, written once, so it works for every row and every item.

checkpoints.text: Make a recipe named `item_cost` with two ingredients, `count` and `price`. It hands back the cost: `count` things at `price` each. Put the recipe at the top, under the two notes.

Use the ingredients, never one line's numbers: `return 3 * 4` hands back 12 for every call.

exercises.title: Trace the call
exercises.martu:
Trace this program in your head, as in Be the ledger. Write down two numbers. One is what the call hands back. The other is what the last line prints:
```python
def ward_strength(lanterns, runes):
    light = lanterns * 10
    glow = runes * 5
    return light + glow

barrier = ward_strength(2, 5) + 10
print(barrier)
```
Use what is IN each box when its line runs, like showing your work in math.
Stuck? Skip this task, or go back to the lesson Recipes With Names. Tasks you pass here stay ✓ done.

```text
ward_strength(5, 4)
  lanterns = 5
  runes = 4
  light = 50
  glow = 20
  return 70 ----+
                |
barrier = 70 + 10
```

2. Work out `light` and `glow` from what is IN `lanterns` and `runes`.
3. `return` hands back `light + glow`.
4. The last line adds 10, and `print` shows `barrier`.

Write your own skill check as a recipe, like the trap-door checks in the campaign. First pick how hard it is. Then hand back `True` when the roll is high enough, and `False` when it isn't. A roll of exactly `needed` counts as high enough. I test it with every kind of roll.

anotherWay.text:
```text
1 ... needed-1 | needed ... 20
     False     |    True
```

1. Set `needed = ` to a number from 2 to 20.
2. `roll >= needed` is `True` or `False`.
3. Hand it back with `return`. The long way, `if` / `return True` / `else:` / `return False`, works too.

items.title: Quick Check Recipes I · Form A questions
items.summary: Four questions that go with Quick Check Recipes I. To pass the Quick Check, get 3 of the 4 right.

questions.q: Which line makes a box that holds a value?

whyWrong.0: `def` never makes a box. Python stops right away, because it expects `(` after the name.
whyWrong.2: This line starts a recipe, not a box. A recipe holds steps, indented under it, not a value.

questions.explain: A box is a name, then `=`, then a value: `hero = "Lucky"`. Read `=` as *gets*: hero gets Lucky. `def` makes a recipe instead.

The recipe works out 17 in `shield`, but it has no `return`, like an answer worked out on scrap paper and never written on the answer sheet. So the call hands back `None`, and `lucky_shield` holds `None`.
`print(3 * 5)` uses numbers typed into the recipe, not its ingredients, so every call shows 15. To use the 2 and the 9 that the call hands over, the recipe needs `count * price`.
`.lower()` makes every letter small. Then `.capitalize()` makes only the first letter big, like Format, then Capitalization, then Sentence case in Google Docs.

exercises.martu:
Trace this program in your head, as in Be the ledger. Write down two numbers. One is what the call hands back. The other is what the last line prints:
```python
def glow_total(candles, runes):
    light = candles * 4
    shine = runes * 3
    return light + shine

room = glow_total(5, 3) + 10
print(room)
```

items.title: Quick Check Recipes I · Form B questions
items.summary: Four questions that go with Quick Check Recipes I. To pass the Quick Check, get 3 of the 4 right.

questions.q: Which line makes a box that holds a value?

whyWrong.0: `def` never makes a box. Python stops right away, because it expects `(` after the name.
whyWrong.2: This line starts a recipe, not a box. A recipe holds steps, indented under it, not a value.

questions.explain: A box is a name, then `=`, then a value: `spell = "Fireball"`. Read `=` as *gets*: spell gets Fireball. `def` makes a recipe instead.
The recipe works out 15 in `fuel`, but it has no `return`, like an answer worked out on scrap paper and never written on the answer sheet. So the call hands back `None`, and `tank` holds `None`.
`print(6 + 2)` uses numbers typed into the recipe, not its ingredients, so every call shows 8. To use the 4 and the 5 that the call hands over, the recipe needs `base + bonus`.
`.lower()` makes every letter small. Then `.capitalize()` makes only the first letter big, like Format, then Capitalization, then Sentence case in Google Docs.

items.title: Mar'tu's Chalk Notes: Recipes
items.summary: Every idea from Unit 3 on one page, with a short example of each. You can print it.

entries.note: `def` makes a recipe (a function): a set of steps with a name, indented under it. Making it runs nothing, the way f(x) = 2x works nothing out until you write f(13). Write its name with `()` to call it. (Lesson: Recipes With Names)

entries.concept: `=` makes a box, `def` makes a recipe
entries.note: A box holds a value. A recipe holds steps. `def` never makes a box.
`pass` means do nothing. It holds the spot, like a blank recipe card, until you replace it with real steps, indented. You've seen this at the cabin door: `move_left()` with `party.move("left")`.

entries.concept: Ingredients and what you hand over
entries.output:
Lucky, get inside!
Bomb Shell, get inside!
entries.note: `hero_name` is the ingredient (parameter): a named blank, like the blank in a sentence frame, "____, get inside!" `"Lucky"` is what you hand over (argument). Each call fills the blank again.

entries.concept: Use the ingredients, never one call's numbers
entries.note: Write the math with the ingredient names, like a formula: area = length × width works for any rectangle. `print(4 + 3)` inside would show 7 for every call.

`return` hands the answer back to the line that called, like writing it on the answer sheet. The call is replaced by what comes back, the way f(13) is replaced by 26. `lucky_max = ...` catches it in a box.
`print` only says the answer out loud. With no `return`, the call hands back `None`, Python's word for nothing. `None` is not 0.
Hand back the box this recipe made, `total`. A name from an example, like `result`, does not exist in this recipe.

Like showing your work in math, write down what each box holds: lamps 4, nights 2, oil 8, spare 6. The call hands back 14, so `stock` is 15. Use what is IN the boxes. (Lesson: Recipes With Names, Be the ledger)

Call the helper (the recipe that hands back the line), store what it hands back in a box (a variable), then pass that box on, like basketball: catch the ball, then pass it on. You've seen this: `present_dialogue_option()`.
`.lower()` makes every letter small. `.capitalize()` makes only the first letter big, like Format, then Capitalization, then Sentence case in Google Docs.
`roll >= needed` is already `True` or `False`, so hand it back. An `if` with `return True` and `else:` `return False` does the same. You've seen this: `return roll >= required_roll`.
The ingredient decides how many faces the die has: `roll_die(6)` rolls a d6, a die with 6 faces. You've seen this: `perform_roll(die_size)`.
Python's last line: SyntaxError: expected '('. *Syntax* means grammar: Python can't read this line. `def` makes recipes. A box is `max_mana = 18`.
Python's last line: SyntaxError: expected ':'. A `def` line ends with `:`, like the heading of an outline before its points.
Python's last line: IndentationError: expected an indented block after function definition. A recipe needs at least one indented line under its `def` line, even `pass`.
Python's last line: NameError: name 'say_ready' is not defined. Python reads from the top down, like a page in a book, so put the `def` above the call.
Python's last line: TypeError: show_hit() missing 1 required positional argument: 'bonus'. A *positional argument* is a value you hand over. Hand over one value for each ingredient.

entries.concept: Error: a name from an example
entries.note: Python's last line: NameError: name 'result' is not defined. Hand back this recipe's own box: `return total`.
No error, and nothing runs. A recipe's name alone is not a call: add `()`. If you print it, you see `<function say_ready ...>`.
